Family Health

Prostatitis: infection, pelvic pain and treatment

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The prostate is a small gland below the bladder, surrounding the urethra and contributing fluid to semen. Prostatitis describes inflammation or related prostate-area symptoms. Some cases are bacterial infections; many persistent pelvic pain cases are not. The type matters because antibiotics do not treat every cause.

Four types, with different causes

Acute bacterial prostatitis starts suddenly and can make you very unwell. Chronic bacterial prostatitis involves persistent or recurrent bacterial infection, often with repeated urinary infections. Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS) involves ongoing pelvic pain without a demonstrated bacterial cause. Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis is found incidentally without symptoms and often needs no treatment.

Bacteria may reach the prostate from the urinary tract; catheter use, urinary procedures, obstruction or previous urinary infection can contribute. Some infections are sexually transmitted. In CP/CPPS, muscle tension, nerve sensitivity and immune or other pain mechanisms may interact; a previous infection does not prove continuing infection.

Symptoms and when to get help

Possible symptoms include burning, frequency, urgency, night-time urination, a weak stream or difficulty starting, and pain in the lower abdomen, back, groin, penis, testicles or between the scrotum and anus. Ejaculation may hurt. Acute infection can also cause fever, chills, nausea, vomiting and body aches. Cloudiness or odor alone cannot diagnose infection.

Seek same-day assessment for new painful urinary symptoms, particularly with fever or feeling ill, and for visible or suspected blood in urine even once, in a small amount or when uncertain. Complete inability to urinate needs immediate emergency care. Confusion, severe breathing difficulty, blue/pale/blotchy skin, fainting or rapidly worsening severe illness also need emergency help. Do not wait several days. Seek immediate emergency help if you are breathing very fast, have slurred or incoherent speech, have a rash that does not fade when pressed, or think you may have sepsis. You do not need to have every sign.

Persistent and recurring pelvic pain

Chronic bacterial infection may produce milder symptoms that return, including recurrent urinary infections, pain and painful ejaculation. CP/CPPS can affect the same areas, with symptoms fluctuating and affecting sleep, work, sexual function and wellbeing. The chronic label commonly describes symptoms lasting at least three months; it is not a reason to delay assessment.

Pain is real even when cultures show no infection. A clinician should consider other urinary, genital, bowel or musculoskeletal causes and assess pelvic floor tenderness, stress and the impact on daily life. Several mechanisms can coexist, so one treatment may not address everything.

How clinicians investigate

Assessment starts with symptoms, previous infections or procedures, medicines, supplements and sexual history. With explanation and consent, examination may include the abdomen, genitals, groin nodes and a gentle rectal examination of the prostate. A rectal examination alone cannot exclude cancer. Do not massage the prostate during suspected acute bacterial prostatitis: it can spread bacteria into the blood.

For suspected acute infection, a midstream urine culture is important, ideally before antibiotics without delaying necessary treatment in severe illness. Blood tests or cultures may be needed if unwell; STI testing is selected according to risk. In non-acute cases, a specialist may use urine samples before and after prostate massage to localize bacteria. This is not a home procedure.

Other tests and PSA

Ultrasound or other imaging may be used for a suspected abscess, obstruction or another diagnosis. Cystoscopy and urine-flow or bladder-function tests are selective, not routine for everyone. Semen testing alone is not the usual diagnostic approach; a prostate biopsy is not a routine prostatitis test and should not be performed during untreated bacterial infection.

Inflammation can raise PSA, so it is not a useful test for diagnosing active prostatitis and does not itself diagnose cancer. Testing or repeat testing should be timed after infection has settled, according to the individual situation. A persistently raised result needs appropriate assessment, not automatic longer antibiotics or a biopsy solely because a fixed one-to-three-month interval has passed.

Treating bacterial prostatitis

Bacterial prostatitis needs a prescribed antibiotic chosen for the organism, local resistance, previous treatment, allergies and ability to reach the prostate. NICE advises reviewing acute treatment after 14 days, with another 14 days if needed; EAU describes a total of two to four weeks for acute infection and commonly four to six weeks for chronic bacterial infection. These are clinical frameworks, not personal prescriptions or a universal six-month course.

Severe infection may require hospital care, intravenous antibiotics and fluids. Retention needs clinical drainage, and an abscess may need a procedure. Take treatment as prescribed and attend review. If acute symptoms are not starting to improve within 48 hours, seek urgent reassessment; get help sooner for worsening or severe illness. Recurrence needs a review of cultures, resistance, obstruction or other causes rather than repeatedly using leftover antibiotics.

Antibiotics are not every pelvic pain treatment

AUA 2025 guidance discourages empirical prolonged antibiotics for CP/CPPS without evidence of infection. EAU allows a selected initial course in some previously untreated primary prostate pain cases, but emphasizes avoiding unnecessary antibiotics and changing approach after failure. Your clinician should explain the rationale; repeatedly treating negative-culture pain as infection can delay useful care.

Treatment usually combines options matched to symptoms. Alpha blockers such as silodosin can relax muscles and help selected urinary symptoms; they are not antibiotics and do not shrink the prostate. Anti-inflammatory pain medicines such as ibuprofen or aspirin are not antibiotics either. Suitability, interactions, stomach or kidney problems and other risks need review; do not start a drug combination yourself.

Other medicines need careful selection

Muscle relaxants such as cyclobenzaprine, benzodiazepines such as clonazepam, and medicines targeting nerve pain are not antibiotics. Some are considered for selected symptoms, but benefits are uncertain or limited and side effects matter. Benzodiazepines can cause sedation, dependence and dangerous withdrawal; do not start or suddenly stop them without a prescribing plan.

Glycosaminoglycan-related products, including chondroitin, are also not antibiotics. Evidence and indications vary, and treatments studied for bladder pain must not automatically be applied to prostate pain. Supplements can interact with medicines. Prostate surgery is not a routine cure for CP/CPPS; procedures are reserved for a clear indication such as an abscess or obstruction.

Physical and psychological support

A pelvic health physiotherapist can assess overactive or tender muscles and offer relaxation, selected manual techniques or biofeedback. Biofeedback helps you recognize muscle activity; it is not a guaranteed cure. Repeated strengthening exercises or Kegels may worsen an overactive pelvic floor, so follow an individual assessment rather than assuming everyone should strengthen.

Warm baths or protected gentle heat may ease discomfort; avoid burns and prostate self-massage. Acupuncture may help selected people. Relaxation, paced breathing, stress-management skills or cognitive behavioral therapy can support pain coping alongside medical care. These approaches do not mean the pain is imagined, and no single complementary treatment reliably cures every case.

Daily habits, sex and follow-up

Drink enough to avoid dehydration without forcing large volumes or assuming water clears infection. Caffeine, alcohol, spicy or acidic foods may trigger symptoms in some people; a symptom diary can guide personal adjustments rather than a universal restrictive diet. Seek support for persistent pain, mood changes or sexual difficulties.

Prostatitis is not automatically contagious, but an STI can cause related infection. If an STI is suspected or confirmed, follow sexual-health advice about testing, partner assessment and treatment; avoid sex until the advised treatment period is complete, symptoms have resolved and partners are treated. Otherwise adapt sexual activity if painful. Persistent symptoms or blood in semen still merit assessment; do not assume they are always harmless.

Complications and outlook

Acute bacterial prostatitis can cause urinary retention, an abscess, bacteria in the bloodstream and sepsis, which can be fatal without timely treatment. Chronic conditions may cause ongoing urinary problems, painful ejaculation, sexual difficulties and pelvic pain. Early assessment and a clear follow-up plan matter, even if symptoms seem mild.

Bacterial infection often improves with appropriate treatment, but recurrence needs investigation. CP/CPPS may require several coordinated treatments and ongoing adjustment, without a guaranteed cure date. Prostatitis is not prostate cancer; overlapping symptoms or an abnormal PSA still need assessment, and an earlier prostatitis diagnosis does not rule out another condition.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current EAU and NICE bacterial-prostatitis guidance supports culture-informed treatment, clinical review and urgent care for retention, abscess or severe infection. Antibiotic durations differ by type and response.

AUA 2025 and EAU chronic-pain guidance support individualized care; they differ on selected initial empirical antibiotics, while repeated unnecessary courses should be avoided. Pelvic relaxation and other treatments depend on assessment.

NHS and NIDDK warning signs support immediate emergency care for complete retention or sepsis symptoms. NCI explains that inflammation can raise PSA without diagnosing cancer.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record urinary symptoms, pain, temperature, medicines and questions for follow-up. It cannot identify the prostatitis type, interpret PSA, select antibiotics or replace urgent assessment.

When to seek help

Get immediate emergency help for complete inability to urinate, confusion, severe breathing difficulty, fainting or rapidly worsening severe illness. Seek same-day advice for painful urinary symptoms with or without fever, or for blood in urine even once, small or uncertain. Acute symptoms not starting to improve within 48 hours of antibiotics need urgent reassessment; worsening needs help sooner. Do not self-prescribe, massage the prostate or abruptly stop a benzodiazepine. Seek immediate emergency help if you are breathing very fast, have slurred or incoherent speech, have a rash that does not fade when pressed, or think you may have sepsis. You do not need to have every sign.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Prostatitis includes bacterial infections and persistent pelvic pain without demonstrated infection; treatment depends on the type.
  • Complete inability to urinate or sepsis signs need emergency care; new painful urinary symptoms and blood in urine need same-day advice.
  • Antibiotic choice and duration are individualized. Silodosin, pain medicines, muscle relaxants and chondroitin are not antibiotics.
  • Chronic pain care may combine medicines, specialist pelvic therapy and coping support; avoid repeated unnecessary antibiotics, prostate self-massage and automatic Kegels.

Frequently asked questions

What causes prostatitis?

Bacterial forms may follow a urinary infection or urinary procedure, and some related infections are sexually transmitted. Many chronic pelvic pain cases have no demonstrated bacterial cause; muscle, nerve, immune and other pain mechanisms may contribute.

What symptoms should I watch for?

Burning, urinary frequency or difficulty, pelvic or genital pain and painful ejaculation are possible. Fever, chills, vomiting or feeling very ill suggest urgent assessment. Complete inability to urinate, severe breathing difficulty, confusion or fainting needs immediate emergency care. Seek immediate emergency help if you are breathing very fast, have slurred or incoherent speech, have a rash that does not fade when pressed, or think you may have sepsis. You do not need to have every sign.

How is it diagnosed?

History, examination and appropriate urine testing are central; blood or STI tests depend on the situation. Imaging and specialist tests are selective. PSA, semen testing or biopsy are not routine ways to diagnose prostatitis. Prostate massage is unsafe during acute bacterial infection.

How long do antibiotics take?

Duration depends on the bacterial diagnosis, response and medicine. Acute treatment is commonly two to four weeks with review; chronic bacterial treatment is often four to six weeks. Do not choose a course yourself or assume every prostatitis case needs antibiotics for months.

Are silodosin or clonazepam antibiotics?

No. Silodosin is an alpha blocker; clonazepam is a benzodiazepine. Anti-inflammatory drugs, cyclobenzaprine, nerve-pain medicines and chondroitin are not antibiotics either. They have different uses and risks; clonazepam must not be stopped abruptly without professional advice.

Should I do Kegels or massage the prostate?

Not automatically. An overactive pelvic floor may need relaxation rather than strengthening. A trained physiotherapist can assess this. Do not massage your prostate yourself; massage during acute bacterial prostatitis can spread infection.

Does prostatitis mean cancer or an STI?

No, but symptoms can overlap with other conditions. PSA can rise with inflammation and needs individual follow-up. If an STI is suspected or found, sexual-health testing, partner care and the advised period without sex are important; not all prostatitis is sexually transmitted.

What if treatment is not helping?

For acute infection, seek urgent reassessment if symptoms are not starting to improve within 48 hours, and sooner if worsening. Recurring infection or persistent pain needs a review of the diagnosis and treatment plan. Complete retention or sepsis signs need immediate emergency help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
